questions.question: Find the odd one out with respect to animals’ response to abiotic factors.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Reproduce**__.

__
 
• The factor to which the animal's response is reproduce is a biotic factor.
 
• So, the correct option is** Reproduce.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **Key Points__**

__
 
• There are two types of factors affecting the ecosystem:
 
 
• **Biotic factors **
 
• **Abiotic factors**
 
 
 
• **Biotic factors** are the living parts of an ecosystem that shapes its environment.
 
• Some common biotic factors are** consumers, producers, herbivores, carnivores, omnivores, and decomposers.**
 
• **Abiotic factors **are non-living parts of an ecosystem that shapes its environment. 
 
• Five common abiotic factors are** atmosphere, temperature/ sunlight, water, chemical elements, and wind.**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__ **

 
• An ecosystem is a place where the living and nonliving components 'interact with each other.
 
• **Type of ecosystems**:
 
 
• **Aquatic Ecosystem: Freshwater ecosystem, Marine ecosystem**
 
• **Terrestrial Ecosystem: Forest ecosystem, Grassland ecosystem, Tundra ecosystem, and Desert ecosystem.**
 
 
 
• The largest ecosystem in the world is the aquatic ecosystem. It constitutes 70% of the surface of the earth.

questions.question: Select the INCORRECT statement with regards to vitamins.

options.text: Plants can synthesise almost all vitamins.
Most of the vitamins cannot get synthesised in sufficient amount in our body.
Some bacteria in the gut do not produce vitamins.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**some bacteria in the gut do not produce vitamins**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Plants can synthesize almost all vitamins, making them a **primary source of vitamins** for many organisms.
 
• Most vitamins cannot be synthesized in sufficient amounts in our body, necessitating their intake through diet.
 
• Vitamins are organic compounds essential for normal growth and nutrition, usually required in small quantities in the diet.
 
• Some bacteria in the gut do produce vitamins, such as **Vitamin K and certain B vitamins**, contributing to the host's nutritional needs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Vitamins are classified into two categories: **fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) and water-soluble (B-complex and C)**.
 
• Deficiency of vitamins can lead to various health issues, such as** scurvy (Vitamin C deficiency), rickets (Vitamin D deficiency), and beriberi (Vitamin B1 deficiency)**.
 
• The human body requires vitamins for various biochemical and physiological functions, including immune function, energy production, and bone health.
 
• While the body can store fat-soluble vitamins, water-soluble vitamins need to be consumed more regularly as they are not stored and are excreted in urine.

questions.question: In which year did a trio of scientists, Avery, MacLeod and McCarty, prove that except viruses, all living organisms have DNA as their genetic material?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1944**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In 1944, Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty conducted experiments that demonstrated that DNA is the substance that causes bacterial transformation.
 
• Their findings provided critical evidence that DNA is the hereditary material in organisms, excluding viruses, which can have RNA as their genetic material.
 
• This was one of the first significant steps in molecular biology that led to the identification of DNA as the carrier of genetic information.
 
• Their work built upon Frederick Griffith's experiment in 1928, which suggested the existence of a "transforming principle" that could transfer genetic information.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid)**

 
 
• DNA is a molecule that carries most of the genetic instructions used in the growth, development, functioning, and reproduction of all known living organisms and many viruses.
 
• DNA is composed of two strands that coil around each other to form a double helix, carrying the genetic instructions in sequences of four types of nucleotides: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), and guanine (G).
 
 
 
• **RNA (Ribonucleic Acid)**
 
 
• RNA is a molecule essential in various biological roles in coding, decoding, regulation, and expression of genes.
 
• RNA is usually single-stranded and is composed of nucleotides: adenine (A), uracil (U), cytosine (C), and guanine (G).
 
• In some viruses, RNA acts as the genetic material instead of DNA.
 
 
 
• **Bacterial Transformation**
 
 
• Bacterial transformation is a process by which bacterial cells take up foreign DNA molecules and incorporate them into their own genetic material, leading to genetic changes.
 
• This process was first observed by Frederick Griffith in 1928, which led to the discovery of the "transforming principle" later identified as DNA by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty.
 
 
 
• **Griffith's Experiment**
 
 
• Griffith's experiment demonstrated that a substance from dead bacteria could genetically transform living bacteria.
 
• He worked with two strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae: a virulent S strain with a smooth capsule and a non-virulent R strain without a capsule.
 
• His results showed that heat-killed S strain bacteria could transfer genetic material to the R strain, making it virulent.

questions.question: The bacterium flagellum is composed of three major structural elements. Which of the following is NOT one of these elements?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Torso**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Bacterium Flagella**

 
 
• Bacterial flagella are **made of the protein flagellin and are a coiled, thread-like structure with a sharp bend and a rotary motor at the base**.
 
• It gives bacteria the **ability to swim freely **through a binary compound of aqueous, also known as **motility or self-propulsion**. 
 
• It is composed of **three major** structural elements;
 
 
• **Basal body**
 
 
• It is joined to the **cytoplasmic membrane and cell membrane**.

 It is made up of **rings **that are surrounded by **MotB proteins**.
 
 
 
• **Hook**
 
 
• A hook is the name for the **wider area at the base of the flagellum**.
 
• It connects the** filament to the base's motor protein**.
 
 
 
• **Filament**
 
 
• It is a** ****thin, hair-like structure** emerging from the hook.
 
 
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://www.oercommons.org/editor/images/2358] 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The long, helical filament of bacterial flagella is made up of **several flagellin subunits organised in a variety of tangled chains**.
 
• A flagellum is made up of **numerous parts and rotates**, similar to a boat motor's propeller.
 
• Depending on the species, the diameter of bacterial flagella varies, which lies between 15 and 20 nm.
 
• **Functions of Bacterial Flagella**
 
 
• Role in pathogenesis
 
• Organ of locomotion
 
• Role in identification of organism

questions.question: Which protein acts like a binder, holding food together and adding a ‘stretch’ property, and is found naturally in some grains, including wheat, barley, and rye?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gluten**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Gluten**

 
 
• Gluten protein acts like a binder, holding food together and adding a ‘stretch’ property. 
 
• It is found naturally in some grains, including wheat, barley, and rye.
 
• **Wheat and foods containing wheat **are widely available in our food supply and are most often associated to gluten.
 
• The** 75–85% of the total protein** in bread wheat is made up of gluten.
 
• Glutens, particularl**y Triticeae glutens, have exceptional viscoelastic and adhesive qualities** that give **dough its elasticity, aid in rising and maintaining its shape, and frequently result in a chewy texture **in the final product.
 
• Some people may experience** negative, inflammatory, immune, and autoimmune reactions** when exposed to gluten.
 
• The spectrum of gluten-related disorders includes **dermatitis herpetiformis, gluten ataxia, and other neurological conditions, as well as celiac disease, which affects 1-2% of the general population and non-celiac gluten sensitivity, which affects 0.5–13% of the general population**.
 
• The** gluten-free diet** is used to treat these disorders.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Prolamin**

 
 
• A class of** plant storage proteins known as prolamins **has a high concentration of the proline amino acid.
 
• They are present in plants, primarily in the** seeds of cereal grains such oats (avenin), corn, wheat, zein, barley (hordein), rye, and sorghum**.
 
• They are characterized by a** high proline and glutamine content **as well as a poor water solubility.
 
 
 
• **Albumin**
 
 
• The most popular** albumins are the serum albumins**, which belong to a family of globular proteins. 
 
• All of the albumin family's proteins are** heat-denatured, water soluble and moderately soluble in concentrated salt solutions**.
 
• The **liver **produces the protein albumin.
 
 
 
• **Glycinin**
 
 
• The main** soybean seed protein **known as glycinin has been recognised as an important food **allergen**.
 
• With the exception of the acidic polypeptide A4, glycinin is a** hexameric protein made up of alternating acidic and basic units around the ring and connected by disulfide bridges**.

questions.question: How do humans acclimatise at high altitudes where atmospheric pressure is low for normal breathing?

options.text: By decreasing red blood cell production, decreasing the binding affinity of haemoglobin and by increasing breathing rate
By increasing red blood cell production, decreasing the binding affinity of haemoglobin and by increasing breathing rate
By increasing white blood cell production, decreasing the binding affinity of haemoglobin and by increasing breathing rate

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By increasing red blood cell production, decreasing the binding affinity of haemoglobin and by increasing breathing rate**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Acclimatisation**

 
 
• **Acclimatisation** is the l**ong-term adaptation to high altitude**, which is primarily carried on **by an increase in red blood cell production and capillary tissue perfusion**.
 
• At high altitudes, acclimatisation typically **takes 1-3 days**.
 
• The b**ody undergoes a number of adaptations** that enable it to **function with less oxygen **at high altitudes, such as:
 
 
• the** depth of breathing increases **or by increasing breathing rate.
 
• Increased **pulmonary arterial pressure "forces" blood into areas of the lung** that are typically not used when breathing at sea level.
 
• The **body creates more red blood cells to transport oxygen**, as well as more of an enzyme. 
 
• By decreasing the **binding affinity of haemoglobin**.
 
 
 
• In order to reduce the **effects of altitude sickness and to balance out increased urination, it's critical to stay hydrated during acclimatisation**.
 
• Despite acclimation, the **heart rate and ventilation rate both rise when at rest, **whereas the heart rate falls when ** at its highest degree of activity due to the release of oxygen from haemoglobin to the body's tissues**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Altitude Sickness**

 
 
• At sea level, **there are around 21% more oxygen** molecules than usual.
 
• While the **concentration does not change with the increase in altitude but the amount of oxygen molecules per breath and the atmospheric pressure decreases**.
 
• At **12,000 feet (3,658 metres)**, there are around **40% less oxygen **molecules in each breath.
 
• Even while at rest, **your breathing rate needs to increase for the body to receive enough oxygen**.
 
• Continued exposure to **higher altitudes without enough acclimatisation might result in very serious, even fatal illnesses**.

questions.question: Which vitamin is synthesised in the presence of sunlight in our body?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vitamin D.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Vitamin D:-**

 
 
• **It is the vitamin that is synthesized in the presence of sunlight in our body.**
 
• When the skin is exposed to sunlight, a type of cholesterol present in the skin is converted into vitamin D.
 
• Vitamin D is essential for bone health as it helps the body absorb calcium and phosphorus.
 
• Deficiency of vitamin D can lead to rickets in children and osteoporosis in adults.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vitamin B: **

 
 
• There are several types of vitamin B such as B1, B2, B6, B12, etc.
 
• These vitamins are essential for maintaining good health and well-being.
 
• They play a crucial role in the metabolism of energy, red blood cell production, and brain function.
 
 
 
• **Vitamin C: **
 
 
• Also known as ascorbic acid, vitamin C is an antioxidant that helps protect cells from damage caused by free radicals.
 
• It is also important for the growth and repair of tissues in the body.
 
 
 
• **Vitamin A: **
 
 
• This vitamin is important for maintaining good vision, skin health, and immune function.
 
• It is found in animal products such as liver, fish, and eggs, as well as in some plant-based foods like carrots and sweet potatoes.

questions.question: Vitamin B Complex consists of how many vitamins?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**8**__.

__**Explanation:**__

__
 
• **The B complex consists of eight water-soluble vitamins that perform essential and closely related roles in the body's cellular function**__.
 
• These include thiamine (**vitamin B1**), riboflavin (**vitamin B2**), niacin (**vitamin B3**), pantothenic acid (**vitamin B5**), pyridoxine (**vitamin B6**), **biotin **(vitamin B7),** folic acid **(vitamin B9), and cobalamins (**vitamin B12**)

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• B vitamins play a vital role in maintaining good health and well-being. As the building blocks of a healthy body, B vitamins have a direct impact on your energy levels, **brain function, and cell metabolism**.
 
• B vitamins are especially important for women who are pregnant and breastfeeding. These vitamins aid in fetal brain development as well as reduce the risk of birth defects.
 
• And for expectant mothers, B vitamins may boost energy levels, ease nausea, and **lower the risk of developing preeclampsia**.
 
• B vitamins are thought to increase testosterone levels in men, which naturally decrease with age. They may also help men build muscle and increase strength. However, human studies confirming these claims are lacking. 
 
• Each member of the B-complex has a unique structure and performs unique functions in the human body.
 
• **Vitamins B1, B2, B3, and biotin participate in different aspects of energy production, vitamin B6 is essential for amino acid metabolism, and vitamin B12 and folic acid facilitate steps required for cell division.**

questions.question: Phytoplankton, small sea-dwelling organisms, belong to which trophic level of the food web?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Primary producers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Phytoplankton**, also known as **microalgae**, are similar to **terrestrial plants **in that they contain **chlorophyll **and **require sunlight **in order to **live and grow**.
 
• **Most phytoplankton **is **buoyant **and **floats **in the **upper part of the ocean**, where **sunlight penetrates the water**.
 
• **Autotrophs **or **primary producers **are **organisms **that acquire **their energy from sunlight **and **materials from nonliving sources**.
 
• **Algae**, **higher plants**, and **some bacteria **and protists are important **autotrophs in running waters**.
 
• **Heterotrophs **obtain **energy **and **materials **by **consuming living **or **dead organic matter**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Primary consumers **make up the **second trophic level**. They are also called **herbivores**. They eat **primary producers**—**plants or algae**—and **nothing else**. For example, a **grasshopper **living in the **Everglades **is **a primary consumer**.
 
• The **organisms **that **eat the primary consumers **are **meat eaters **(carnivores) and are **called secondary consumers**. The **secondary consumers **tend to be **larger and fewer in number**. This **continues **on, all the way up to the **top of the food chain**.
 
• **Decomposers **feed on **dead things**: **dead plant **materials such as **leaf litter **and **wood, animal carcasses, and faeces**. They perform a **valuable service as Earth's cleanup crew**. Without **decomposers**, **dead leaves**, **dead insects**, and **dead animals **would **pile up everywhere.**

questions.question: What is a way in which adaptation does NOT take place?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **__Emotional__**.

**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• Emotional adaptation **clustered with positive traits and an outward focus and was negatively associated with negative traits and an inward focus**
 
• Emotional adaptation was conceptually located in close proximity to active and adaptive coping, and furthest away from maladaptive coping.
 
• They are **efficient, coordinated responses **that help organisms **to reproduce, protect offspring, maintain cooperative alliances, and to avoid physical threats.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

__
 
• **​__****Physiological adaptation** **refers to the**** internal organs, tissues, and cells**. In this type of adaptation, the cellular features, internal organs, changes in the hormonal level, mood swings, and other features help an organism to survive, adapt and respond to the changes in its environment.
 
• **Behavioral adaptation:** **something an animal does usually**** in response to some type of external stimulus in order to survive**. Hibernating during winter is an example of a behavioral adaptation.
 
• **Morphological adaptation** is **a structural change that gives an organism a greater chance of survival in its habitat**.

questions.question: At high doses, ______ kills cancer cells or slows their growth by damaging their DNA. Cancer cells whose DNA is damaged beyond repair stop dividing or die. When the damaged cells die, they are broken down and removed by the body.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Radiation therapy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Radiotherapy to treat cancer:

 
 
• High doses of radiation are used in radiation therapy, also known as radiotherapy, as a cancer treatment to eradicate cancer cells and reduce tumour size.
 
• As with X-rays of your teeth or shattered bones, radiation is utilised at low doses in x-rays to see inside your body.
 
• Radiation therapy damages cancer cells' DNA, which either kills them or limits their growth at high dosages.
 
• Cancer cells that have DNA damage that cannot be repaired either cease proliferating or die.
 
• When the injured cells expire, the body degrades and eliminates them.
 
• But too much radiation can damage tissues by changing cell structure and damaging DNA.
 
• This can cause serious health problems.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chemotherapy **

 
 
• Chemotherapy is the use of any drug to treat any disease.
 
• But to most people, the word chemotherapy means drugs used for** cancer treatment**. 
 
• It's often shortened to “chemo.” Surgery and radiation therapy remove, kill, or damage cancer cells in a certain area, but chemo can work throughout the whole body.
 
 

 
• Surgery:

 
 
• Surgery is a medical speciality that employs operative manual and instrumental techniques on a patient to examine or treat a pathological condition.
 
• Such as a disease or injury, to enhance bodily function or appearance, or to repair unwelcome ruptured areas
 
 
 
• **Physiotherapy**
 
 
• ​Physiotherapy is a healthcare profession that aims to help people restore and maintain movement and function when affected by** injury**, **illness** or **disability**.
 
• Physiotherapists use a combination of manual **therapy**, **exercise**, and **education**.

questions.question: ______ is generally called as milk sugar as it is found in milk

__
 
• **Lactose**__ is a disaccharide composed of galactose and glucose.
 
• The molecular formula of lactose is **C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁.**
 
• __**The sugar present in milk is called lactose.**__
 
• Lactose is generally called **milk sugar** as it is found in milk.
 
• Lactose is composed of** β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose.**
 
• Lactose is a reducing sugar.
 
• Lactose composes about 2–8% of milk by weight.

• **Fructose** is the sugar present in fruits.
 
 
• Fructose is found in honey, vine fruits, flowers, berries, and most root vegetables.
 
• Fructose was discovered by Augustin-Pierre Dubrunfaut in 1847.
 
 
 
• **Maltose** is a disaccharide formed when two units of glucose molecules are bound together.
 
 
• Maltose is a reducing sugar.
 
 
 
• **Glucose **is a simple sugar and the most abundant monosaccharide.
 
 
• It is mainly made by plants and most algae during photosynthesis from water and carbon dioxide, using energy from sunlight.

questions.question: In 1930, which scientist was awarded the Nobel Prize for describing the human ABO blood group system?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Karl Landsteiner.**__

__
 
• In 1930, Karl Landsteiner was awarded the Nobel Prize for describing the human ABO blood group system

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **Key Points__** 

__
 
• **Karl Landsteiner **discovered human blood groups in the year **1900.**
 
• The discovery laid the foundation for the modern medical practice of blood transfusion.
 
• Karl Landsteiner**​**__ himself considered it an accidental discovery.
 
• On the basis of the presence of **Antigen or Glycoprotein, **there are four groups of blood in human:
 __
 
• That contains Antigen A–Blood **Group A.**
 
• That contains Antigen B–Blood **Group B.**
 
• That contains **both the Antigens A and B**–Blood **Group AB.**
 
• That contains **neither of the Antigens**– Blood **Group O.**
 
 
 
• Blood **Group O** is called the **Universal Donor.**
 
• Blood **Group AB** is called** Universal Receptor.​**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• **The Nobel Prize in Medicine 1974** was awarded jointly to **Albert Claude, Christian de Duve and George E. Palade** "for their discoveries concerning the **structural and functional organization of the cell."**
 
• George Wald with Haldan K. Hartline and Ragnar Granit of Sweden received the** Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine in 1967** for his work on the **chemistry of vision.**
 
• **Roger Guillemin and Andrew Schally** shared the Nobel Prize in** Medicine and Physiology in 1977** for their work on neurohormones.
